A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same StreamV2V research, with matching authors, method, and principal experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original video-generation experiments, DAVIS evaluation metrics, user preferences, runtime measurements, and component ablations in Section 5 and the appendix.

after.justification: v3 retains those original empirical results and adds feature visualizations, memory measurements, and sensitivity analyses in the appendix.

M1.justification: Extended self-attention, feature fusion, similarity masking, and dynamic merging retain the same procedures and defaults. Appendix A.5.2 adds pseudocode documenting the existing merging procedure; the alternative sampling strategies are experimental ablations, not changes to the proposed default method.

E1.justification: Both versions retain DAVIS video editing, the in-house cartoon-style evaluation, webcam and drawing demonstrations, long-video translation, and continuous text-to-image generation. The added resolution and parameter sweeps do not establish a new dataset or task. Participant demographics are newly disclosed rather than evidence of a changed population.

E2.justification: The main comparison retains StreamDiffusion, CoDeF, Rerender, TokenFlow, and FlowVid. New Table 6 evaluates uniform-grid and split sampling against default random sampling, adding comparison strategies within the DyMe ablation without expanding the external baseline set.

E3.justification: The existing benchmark and user-study protocols remain unchanged. Appendix A.8 adds resolution tests from 512×512 to 1536×1536 on a 24-GB A5000, fusion-threshold and update-interval sweeps, and sampling-strategy comparisons. Tables 4-5 specify 19 videos, while retained Section 5.4 specifies 18 in-house videos; their relationship is unexplained, so this does not establish a revision of the earlier experiment.

E4.justification: v3 substantially extends diagnostic evaluation: Appendix A.8 tests resolution-dependent memory overhead, fusion thresholds, bank-update frequency, and DyMe sampling choices. New PCA feature visualizations and merging visualizations in A.3.1 and A.5.1 examine the proposed mechanisms. Existing component, bank-size, fusion-position, and denoising-step ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions already report user-study means and standard deviations from at least three participants per comparison. Both describe ten runtime runs, discarding the two highest and two lowest before averaging six. The added analyses introduce no new seed, repeated-run, confidence-interval, or significance-testing practice.

E6.justification: Main benchmark values, user preferences, runtimes, and earlier ablation results remain unchanged. Tables 3-6 add substantial diagnostic results: memory overhead rises from 10% at 512×512 to 136% at 1536×1536; threshold 0.9 gives warp error 73.4; update interval 8 gives 72.4 versus 73.4 for default 4; random, uniform-grid, and split sampling give 73.4, 73.7, and 74.2. These are additional findings, not improvements to retained benchmark scores.

T1.justification: Equations (1)-(2), feature definitions, and the matching and averaging mathematics remain unchanged. Figure 2(c) schematically restates the existing fixed-bank versus batch-memory argument using O(1) and O(N); it adds no substantive derivation, formal assumption, theorem, or proof.

C1.justification: Section 1 strengthens the priority claim from 'one of the first approaches' to 'the first approach' for real-time streaming video-to-video translation. The central contributions, training-free applicability, speed claims, and conclusion otherwise retain their meaning and scope.

C2.justification: Appendix A.8 newly discusses increasing memory overhead at higher resolutions, conjectures missing memory optimizations, and proposes remedies. It also recommends motion-dependent update frequency and explains split sampling through domination by current-frame features. New visualizations support mechanism interpretations. The existing editing and temporal-consistency limitations remain.

D1.justification: v3 adds DyMe pseudocode, visualization procedures, A5000 hardware information, and user-study demographics: college students aged 20-30 with an approximately 2:1 male-to-female ratio. The abstract and new reproducibility statement explicitly report released code and models, beyond v2's project-page link. These are documentation and access disclosures, not verified external resource changes.

R1.justification: The bibliography is unchanged. However, the stronger 'first approach' claim changes priority positioning, and the experimental descriptions newly credit TokenFlow alongside FlowVid for evaluation precedents. The related-work coverage and comparison with concurrent Live2Diff otherwise remain stable.

P1.justification: v3 makes localized language edits, renames 'Preliminary' to 'Background,' exchanges the runtime and user-study subsection order, and reorganizes appendix subsections. It expands Broad Impacts into an Ethics Statement and adds a Reproducibility Statement. The main narrative and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: The diagnostic presentation expands substantially through a memory-scaling panel in Figure 2, feature and merging visualizations in Figures 13 and 16, Tables 3-6, and a boxed pseudocode listing. Existing visual results are retained, with appendix renumbering and relocation; the runtime and user-study figures exchange positions.

improvement.justification: v3 better supports design choices through new ablations, exposes high-resolution memory limitations, and improves implementation and participant documentation. These are useful incremental gains over v2's retained central evaluation. Reporting weaknesses remain: the new 19-video analyses are not linked clearly to the earlier 18-video set, and Figure 2(c)'s minutes axis conflicts with the four-second discussion. These limitations do not outweigh the added evidence and transparency.
